student_role.name: The newest student in Ichabod's class
student_role.setup: You are the newest student in Ichabod Crane's schoolhouse, and you saw something near the bridge the night he vanished.
student_role.intro: You are the newest student in Ichabod Crane's one-room schoolhouse. The night he vanished, you were out late near the church bridge and saw something you still can't explain. This morning his seat is empty, and the whole valley has a theory. What you saw is only a start. The story is your proof.

characters.name: Hans Van Ripper
characters.description: A practical farmer and Ichabod’s former host.
characters.personality: Blunt, guarded, and impatient with superstition.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows only what the source passages show him doing, seeing, or saying, and the gossip of the valley that the passages report. Was never on the road with Ichabod at night.
characters.speech_style: Plain, direct standard English with no dialect: a practical farmer who says what he means.
never_reveal: Never describe anything he did not see himself in the passages.
Never say what happens to Ichabod or to his horse beyond what the passages show.

Irving's text caricatures Black people in three places: the messenger who brings the party invitation to the schoolhouse, the old musician at the dance, and the people watching the dance from the doors and windows. Never repeat, describe, or joke about any of them. If a student asks about any of them, answer only: that is a good question to talk over with your teacher or parent.

characters.name: Brom Bones
characters.description: Abraham Van Brunt, known as Brom Bones: the boldest rider around Sleepy Hollow, Ichabod's rival for Katrina Van Tassel, and later her husband.
characters.personality: Boastful, playful, and proud of his strength and horsemanship. Quick to laugh and to tease. Slippery and evasive whenever the talk turns to the night Ichabod vanished.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows his own rivalry with Ichabod, his own pranks and boasts, and the gatherings he was part of, only as far as the source passages show. Knows nothing beyond the passages.
characters.speech_style: Loud, confident, plain standard English with no dialect. Short boasts, jokes, and questions turned back on the asker.
never_reveal: Never confirm or deny any rumor about himself; answer with a laugh, a boast, or a change of subject.
Never say who Katrina will choose or marry.
Never claim to know what Katrina says to anyone in private.
Never state as fact what happens to Ichabod.

traits.name: Part of the town's ghost stories
traits.line:
The stories of Brouwer, of Bones, and a whole budget of
others were called to mind; and when they had diligently considered them
all, and compared them with the symptoms of the present case, they shook
their heads, and came to the conclusion that Ichabod had been carried
off by the Galloping Hessian.

traits.name: Famous for his strength
traits.line:
Among these, the most formidable was a burly, roaring, roystering blade,
of the name of Abraham, or, according to the Dutch abbreviation, Brom
Van Brunt, the hero of the country round, which rang with his feats of
strength and hardihood.

traits.name: Blamed for every prank
traits.line:

of awe, admiration, and good-will; and, when any madcap prank or rustic
brawl occurred in the vicinity, always shook their heads, and warranted
Brom Bones was at the bottom of it.

scenes.narration: Morning light reaches the empty schoolhouse. The patched copybook windows and abandoned lessons sit just as they were. Hans Van Ripper examines the small bundle and the books that belonged to Ichabod. The fortune-telling book holds a sheet of foolscap with unfinished verses for Katrina Van Tassel. Beyond the window, searchers have left word of a hat and a shattered pumpkin near the brook and bridge. What disappeared: a schoolteacher, a rival, or the truth between them?
scenes.summary: The morning after the party, Ichabod Crane, the schoolteacher, is missing. His horse comes home without him, and people find his hat and a broken pumpkin near the bridge. The town looks through his few belongings and starts telling stories about what happened to him.

bank.question: What kind of teacher was Ichabod with children who misbehaved?

answers.line:
Truth to
say, he was a conscientious man, and ever bore in mind the golden maxim,
“Spare the rod and spoil the child.”

I would not have it imagined, however, that he was one of those cruel
potentates of the school who joy in the smart of their subjects; on
the contrary, he administered justice with discrimination rather than
severity; taking the burden off the backs of the weak, and laying it on
those of the strong.

scenes.narration: You step back to the evening before Ichabod vanished. The Van Tassel farmhouse glows with lamplight, and the tea table is heaped with cakes, pies, and roasted meats. Ichabod dances with Katrina while Brom Bones sits alone in a corner, watching. On the piazza, pipes glow as neighbors trade ghost stories, and Brom tells one of his own. What did Ichabod carry with him when he left this party?
scenes.summary: The night before Ichabod disappeared, he went to a party at the Van Tassel farm. He ate a big meal, danced with Katrina, and listened to ghost stories, including Brom Bones's story about racing the Headless Horseman. After everyone left, Ichabod talked with Katrina alone, then left looking very sad.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly, warm candlelit interior and porch of a large 1790s Dutch farmhouse in the Hudson Valley on an autumn evening, rich amber and brown tones, period-accurate homespun clothing, figures small and softly rendered with no detailed faces, no readable text. Keep the upper-left area (the left two-fifths of the image, top third) as plain, empty, dark wooden wall in deep shadow, because narration text overlays it. Lower-left foreground (x 4 to 34 percent, y 62 to 90 percent): a long tea table heaped with doughnuts, cakes, pies, sliced ham, and a steaming teapot. Upper center-right (x 46 to 68 percent, y 6 to 30 percent): a half-open lamplit doorway where a tall, thin man in a worn coat lingers beside a young woman in an old-fashioned gold-trimmed dress, both seen from behind in soft silhouette. Right side (x 72 to 94 percent, y 30 to 58 percent): a broad-shouldered young man in a fur cap topped with a fox tail sits alone on a bench in a shadowed corner, arms folded, brooding. Lower center (x 40 to 68 percent, y 60 to 86 percent): an open porch where a circle of old farmers sit smoking, pipe bowls glowing in the dusk, one burly figure leaning forward with a raised hand as if telling a tale. scenes.narration: It is past midnight, and you follow the road Ichabod took home. The hills are dark, clouds hide the stars, and the giant tulip tree known as Major André's tree stands in the middle of the road. Beyond it lie the haunted brook, the sandy hollow, and the church bridge where Brom said the Horseman vanished. What did Ichabod see on this road, and what did he only fear?
scenes.summary: Ichabod rode home alone in the dark. He was scared by a famous old tree, and then a large, silent rider began to follow him. The rider seemed to have no head. Ichabod's saddle fell off during the chase, and at the church bridge the rider threw his head at Ichabod and knocked him down.

storybook.art_style:
One style for every page: a painterly storybook illustration in warm gouache on cream paper, with soft edges and visible brush texture. Gently comic in daylight, shadowy and eerie at night, never gory.
Palette: autumn golds, russet, and moss green by day; deep blue-black, gray mist, and pale moonlight by night, with lantern amber as the warm accent.
Setting: a quiet Dutch farming valley near the Hudson River, about 1790: rolling wooded hills, a brook, split-rail fences, a log schoolhouse, stone farmhouses with low sloping roofs, a small church and its wooden bridge.
Ichabod Crane: very tall and thin, narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, big hands and feet, a small head with large ears, large green glassy eyes, and a long pointed nose; loose, rusty-black clothes. Drawn with affection, like a storybook scarecrow, never mocked cruelly.
The Headless Horseman: only ever a dark cloaked rider on a huge black horse, seen from a distance or in silhouette, with no head and nothing shown at the neck. Never a wound.
Never: words, letters, or numbers in the image; blood or injury; caricatured faces; anything a later page reveals.

Quiet and sleepy, with no people in close view.

bridge.summary: The storyteller remembers hunting squirrels in this valley when he was a boy; the roar of his own gun startled him because the place was so quiet. The valley is called Sleepy Hollow, and the families who live there come from the first Dutch settlers. Some say the place is under a spell. Its people believe in marvels, see strange sights, and hear music and voices in the air, and the valley is full of local tales, haunted places, and superstitions.

bridge.summary: Ichabod is not a cruel teacher, but he does punish students with a birch rod, mostly the tough ones, and tells them they will thank him for it someday. He earns very little, so he lives with his students' families, a week at a time, carrying everything he owns tied up in a cotton handkerchief. He eats an enormous amount. To stay welcome, he helps with farm chores and pets the youngest children. He also teaches singing and is proud of his loud voice in church. The women of the valley admire him as an educated man, and he carries gossip from house to house. He has read Cotton Mather's book about witchcraft in New England, and he firmly believes every word of it.

bridge.summary: Ichabod looks over Van Tassel's rich fields and orchards and daydreams about marrying Katrina, selling the land, and heading west with her and a wagon full of children. Inside, the farmhouse is full of treasures: shining pewter, strings of dried fruit and corn on the walls, polished furniture, and old silver. From that moment, Ichabod thinks only about winning Katrina. It will not be easy. She keeps changing her mind, and she has many other admirers, who watch each other jealously and gang up on any newcomer.

bridge.summary: Brom has been courting Katrina for some time, and people whisper that she does not entirely discourage him. When his horse is tied outside the Van Tassel house on a Sunday night, other young men stay away. Ichabod is no match for Brom's strength, but he is like a bendable stick: he bends but never breaks. He courts Katrina quietly, visiting the farmhouse as her singing teacher, and her easygoing parents let her do as she likes. Once Ichabod starts visiting, Brom's horse stops appearing on Sunday nights, and a bitter feud grows between Brom and the schoolmaster.

bridge.summary: One autumn afternoon, while Ichabod watches over his quiet schoolroom, a messenger on a half-wild colt gallops up to the door. He brings an invitation to a party at the Van Tassels' house that evening. Ichabod rushes the students through their lessons and lets them out an hour early, and the children burst outside, shouting with joy.

bridge.summary: After the dance, Ichabod joins the older men who sit smoking on the porch with old Van Tassel. They tell long stories about the Revolutionary War, which was fought near this neighborhood. Each storyteller has made his own part bigger over the years, and each one believes he helped win the war.

In the dark shadow of the grove, on the margin
of the brook, he beheld something huge, misshapen and towering.

He
appeared to be a horseman of large dimensions, and mounted on a black
horse of powerful frame.

As yet the panic of the steed had given his unskilful rider an apparent
advantage in the chase, but just as he had got half way through the
hollow, the girths of the saddle gave way, and he felt it slipping from
under him.

He seized it by the pommel, and endeavored to hold it firm,
but in vain; and had just time to save himself by clasping old Gunpowder
round the neck, when the saddle fell to the earth, and he heard it
trampled under foot by his pursuer.

Another convulsive kick in the ribs, and
old Gunpowder sprang upon the bridge; he thundered over the resounding
planks; he gained the opposite side; and now Ichabod cast a look behind
to see if his pursuer should vanish, according to rule, in a flash of
fire and brimstone.

Just then he saw the goblin rising in his stirrups,
and in the very act of hurling his head at him.

It encountered his cranium
with a tremendous crash,--he was tumbled headlong into the dust, and
Gunpowder, the black steed, and the goblin rider, passed by like a
whirlwind.

André, who had been taken prisoner hard by; and was universally known

About two hundred yards from the tree, a small brook crossed the road,
and ran into a marshy and thickly-wooded glen, known by the name of
Wiley’s Swamp.

trial.

accept.line:
This
road leads through a sandy hollow shaded by trees for about a quarter
of a mile, where it crosses the bridge famous in goblin story; and just
beyond swells the green knoll on which stands the whitewashed church.

As yet the panic of the steed had given his unskilful rider an apparent
advantage in the chase, but just as he had got half way through the
hollow, the girths of the saddle gave way, and he felt it slipping from
under him.

“If I can
but reach that bridge,” thought Ichabod, “I am safe.”
